doc.title: Marty Napoleon interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York, New York, January 16, 1999

title: Hired by Ben Pollack at $75 a week
summary: Pollack hires Marty despite his poor reading; his wife quits her job and joins him on the road.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: And then you walked in the door.
And I walked in the door.

I’m telling you, there are fantastic stories. So he says, “would you like to try out?” Now I’d just left Bob Astor’s band where I couldn’t read this many notes. You know I didn’t know how to read music. So I went over, and he says, “do you want to try out?” I says, “yeah.” I couldn’t remember, everything was a blur. I didn’t remember seeing guys sitting in the band, nothing. All I saw was a piano and music, when they put the music out, and it had real chords written out. It didn’t have—

No symbols. It had real chords, like charts with chords. So when I sat down I just blacked out. I looked at that and I said forget it, it’s not going to happen. But since I had such a good ear from the time I was like six years old or whatever, or from birth, the band started to play and I played along with them. Now I found out later — first Benny comes over to me after I’d played a few numbers with the band, and he says, “okay, kid, you got the job.” And I’m saying why would this guy hire me? I mean I couldn’t hardly play, I couldn’t read, I didn’t know anything. He says, “You got the job. You get 75 bucks a week and we leave Monday for Philadelphia.” So I called my wife and I said, “Honey, quit your job, we’re going on the road.” She says, “get out of here, what are you talking about?” So I told her what happened. She said, “I don’t believe it. What are you talking about?” You know why she was incredulous? Because I had spoken to my father when I left Bob Astor’s band, I said, “pop, I’m married, I know I’m going to have some kids, I can’t read, I’m not too good a piano player, I’ve got to support my wife.” He says, “don’t worry, I know somebody at Wheeler’s Shipyard, I’ll get you a letter of introduction.” And I carried that letter of introduction for two weeks in my pocket. When I went to the union I had that letter in my pocket, I was going to go to the shipyard to get a job. So when I called my wife I said, “guess what? Quit your job.” She was making forty bucks a week as a dressmaker. She said, “I’m not quitting my job, you’re crazy.” I said, “no honey, we’re going on the road, and no wife of mine is going to work.” I said, “I’m going to support the family.” She said, “why, what are you going to get?” I said, “75 bucks a week.” She almost died. I said, “hello?”

’42. People were making 20 dollars a week, 30 dollars. So I went on the road, and I took my wife with me. She quit her job, she came on the road with me, and the rest is history. Six months later we were in Niagara Falls, well Buffalo, we were playing a theater there. And we played a split week which means when you play the theater date you played seven days. When you did a split week you did three days in one and three days in another and you had one day off because Sunday was like Blue Law days you know. So we had a day off, a Sunday off. So Chuck Max and his wife and my wife and I we rented a car and went to Niagara Falls. I said, “didn’t I tell you I’d take you to Niagara Falls for your honeymoon?”
So it was great, I loved it, it was beautiful.
